.blockquote[Two Paths from the Data-Generating Process]

class: left

.blockquote[Part 1 · Notation that does the heavy lifting]

## Two worlds of regression — sample vs. population

The same equation $y = b_0 + b_1 x + e$ can mean *very* different things depending on whether we read it descriptively or stochastically. Sessions 1–2 already touched this. Today the distinction becomes operational — and we will keep the notation tight throughout the labs.

.pull-left[
### Descriptive regression
$$y_i = b_0 + b_1 x_i + e_i$$

* Data treated as a **population** — no random draws, no stochastic error
* A **summary** of observed data
* $\hat y_i$: conditional mean / fitted value
* $b_0, b_1$: marginal effects, ceteris paribus
* $e_i$: residual — what the line cannot describe

*This was our world in Session 1.*
]

.pull-right[
### Stochastic regression model

$$Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_i + \varepsilon_i$$

* Model for a **data-generating process** (DGP)
* $\beta_0, \beta_1$: **unknown** parameters of the **population**
* $\varepsilon_i \sim (0, \sigma^2)$: stochastic error
* Goal: infer from the **sample** to the population
* Requires **assumptions** (A/B/C) for the inference to be valid

*This is the shift that defines today's session.*
]

.small[**Convention used throughout Labs 1–3** (Stocker style): lowercase Roman letters ($b_0, e_i$) for the descriptive / sample-fitted view; Greek letters ($\beta_0, \varepsilon_i$) for the population / DGP view; hats ($\hat\beta_0, \hat\varepsilon_i$) for sample-based estimates of population quantities.]

.quelle[.small[Stocker (Innsbruck), *Angewandte Ökonometrie* §4.1; `r Citet(bib, "taddy_modern_2023")` ch. 1 on DGP framing.]]

???
* This slide is the notational hinge — once students see this, the rest of the session reads cleanly
* In the Labs we follow the same convention: `b_*` in descriptive contexts (Lab 0), `\beta_*` in inference contexts (Lab 1+), `\hat\beta_*` for estimates
* Speaking line: "The equation is the same. The story behind the equation changes everything."



---
class: left

.blockquote[Part 1 · The model]

## Why model? The conditional expectation E[y|x]

.pull-left[
For a response $y$ and inputs $\mathbf{x}$:

$$\mathbb{E}[y\,|\,\mathbf{x}] = f(\mathbf{x}'\boldsymbol{\beta})$$

`r fa('arrow-right')` **Marginal** distribution (top): the unconditional shape of $y$ — single number for the mean.

`r fa('arrow-right')` **Conditional** expectation (bottom): a *function* of $\mathbf{x}$ — different mean per slice.

<br>

.blockquote[
.small[
All three paths — E1, E2, P — make claims about parts of this conditional distribution.
]
]


]

.pull-right[
```{r marginal-conditional-stack}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 4.5
#| fig-height: 4.8
#| fig-align: center
#| out-width: "100%"
set.seed(20260522)
n <- 2400
tbl <- tibble(
  bathrooms = sample(0:7, n, replace = TRUE,
                     prob = c(0.04, 0.18, 0.40, 0.22, 0.10, 0.04, 0.015, 0.005)),
  home_value = exp(11.2 + 0.32 * bathrooms + rnorm(n, sd = 0.45))
)

p_marg <- ggplot(tbl, aes(home_value)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 35, fill = col_neutral, color = "white") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_dollar(scale = 1e-3, suffix = "k"),
                     limits = c(0, 1.6e6)) +
  labs(x = "Home value", y = "Frequency",
       title = "(a) Marginal distribution") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 10, face = "bold"))

p_cond <- ggplot(tbl, aes(factor(bathrooms), home_value)) +
  geom_boxplot(aes(fill = factor(bathrooms)),
               outlier.size = 0.5,
               outlier.colour = col_neutral) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_dollar(scale = 1e-3, suffix = "k")) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#a8e6cf","#80d6c4","#5fc6b8","#43b3a8",
                               "#3196a8","#2576a0","#1c5594","#502479"),
                    guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "Number of bathrooms", y = "Home value",
       title = "(b) Conditional distribution") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 10, face = "bold"))

cowplot::plot_grid(p_marg, p_cond, ncol = 1, rel_heights = c(1, 1.3))
```
]
.quelle[.small[`r Citet(bib, "taddy_modern_2023")` Ch. 1, Fig. 1.1]]

???
* Mirrors Taddy/Hendrix/Harding 2023 Figure 1.1 — both panels (a) marginal histogram and (b) conditional boxplots by bathrooms
* Marginal mean = one number; conditional mean = a function of bathrooms
* The shift from a single number to a function is what regression IS
* All three paths today work on this conditional distribution — but each extracts something different from it

class: left

.blockquote[Part 1 · The logic]

## Models and Data: An Epistemological Perspective

```{r induction-deduction-svg}
#| echo: false
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-align: center
knitr::include_graphics(xfun::from_root("img","Session3","induction_deduction.svg"))
```

???
* Epistemological framing: every empirical analysis takes a stance on how data and theory relate
* **Induction** (purple, top): data are the *source material* from which a hypothesis is generated — data mining, model training, exploratory pattern discovery
* **Deduction** (red, bottom): data are the *arbiter* that tests an *a-priori* specification — but the specification can take two forms:
  - **E1**: the specification is a *model equation* (the classical assumption-based path; Lab 1)
  - **E2**: the specification is a *research design* (the design-based path; Lab 3)
  - Both are deductive in the epistemological sense — what is pre-committed before seeing data is what counts
* Path **P** uses both moves: induction to learn parameters (training), then deduction to predict new x (testing)
* Path **E** is deductive throughout — the difference between E1 and E2 lies in what is pre-committed: model equation or research design
* No abduction in this scheme — it is not needed for the audience here

.panel[.panel-name[New in Session 3]
### The same line, applied to *method choice*

.pull-left[
`r fa('user', fill='#686868')` **AI User** *(method-level)*

* Picks the textbook method
* Reports $R^2$, p-value, default outputs
* Confuses Path E and Path P
* Optimizes within a given **map** — without knowing it
]

.pull-right[
`r fa('user-gear', fill='#D50006')` **AI Value Creator** *(method-level)*

* Asks: *prediction or intervention?*
* Picks the **path** before the estimator
* Validates the diagnostic, not just the point estimate
* **Chooses the map** — and defends it
]


.blockquote[
.small[
Today's labs make this concrete. **Lab 1** is the diagnostic discipline. **Lab 2** is the prediction discipline. **Lab 3** is the causal discipline. Knowing which to pick is the Value-Creator skill.
]
]
]
.panel[.panel-name[The data dimension]
### Why method choice matters for the data moat

`r fa('rocket', fill='#D50006')` **Proprietary data** alone is not enough — it must be paired with the **right path**:

* Predicting customer churn from your own data → Path **P** with regularization (Lab&nbsp;2 family)
* Estimating the effect of a *new* pricing policy → Path **E2** with experimental design (Lab&nbsp;3 family)

`r fa('triangle-exclamation', fill='#686868')` Pairing the wrong path with great data wastes the moat:

* Lasso on a one-off intervention question gives confident, biased nonsense
* OLS controls on observational data without a DAG yield estimates the CEO cannot defend

.quellePanURL[`r Citet(bib, "thomasAIValueCreators2025")`]
]
]

???
* Three panels: (1) Session 1 framing as recall, (2) the NEW Session 3 framing applied to method choice, (3) why path + data must align
* Key shift from Session 1: Value Creation in Block 3 is no longer just about *data* — it is about the *method-path-decision* itself
* Lab 3's deliverable T_final is exactly the artefact a Value Creator produces: a defensible methodological recommendation


---
class: left

.blockquote[Part 1 · The deeper layer]

## Philosophy Eats AI — the layer beneath every method

```{r philosophy-svg}
#| echo: false
#| out-width: "98%"
#| fig-align: center
knitr::include_graphics(xfun::from_root("img","Session3","philosophy_eats_ai.svg"))
```

???
* Schrage & Kiron (2025): every AI stack rests on philosophical commitments — usually unarticulated, sometimes catastrophically wrong
* Three pillars are theirs (Ontology, Epistemology, Teleology); Ethics is treated separately as a fourth
* **Ontology examples**: Starbucks defined the "Starbucks experience" as connection (not transactions) before designing Deep Brew AI. Amazon Prime ontologically defined "best customers" — not "most profitable" — as the optimization target
* **Epistemology examples**: prediction (Path P) and counterfactual evidence (Path E2) are two different theories of what counts as knowing. Confusing them is the root cause of most bad analytics
* **Teleology examples**: Google's Gemini fiasco — accuracy and diversity goals were misaligned; the model fell to whichever objective dominated
* "The map is not the territory" (Korzybski via Wittgenstein, quoted by Schrage & Kiron): metrics are maps; loyalty is the territory; RFM/NPS/churn are metrics that *might* represent loyalty — or might define it by fiat
* The Translator's job: surface these choices before picking a method
* Forward link: Lab 3 (what counts as causal evidence?), back to Lab 1+2 (what counts as a "good" prediction?)

.blockquote[Part 1 · The DGP]

## Two Paths from the Data-Generating Process

```{r dgp-paths-slide}
#| echo: false
#| out-width: "80%"
#| fig-align: center
knitr::include_graphics(xfun::from_root("img","Session3","DGP-Paths_gemini.svg"))
```

.center[
.small[
Same data, same DGP — two analytical purposes. Path E asks *what is*; Path P asks *what next*.
]
]

???
* Same SVG students see in Lab 1 — recognition cue intentional
* Path E (Explanation/Inference): two sub-questions — E1 "what is the partial effect?" (next slide) and E2 "what would change under intervention?"
* Path P (Prediction): a single goal — generalise to new data
* The DGP is the unobservable urn; data are realisations; methods differ by what they extract from that realisation
* Breiman 2001 was the first to make this dichotomy programmatic ("Two Cultures")

.blockquote[Part 1 · Path E branches]

## Path E has two sub-questions

```{r path-e-branches}
#| echo: false
tibble::tribble(
  ~`Sub-question`,                                       ~Goal,                              ~Identification,                                    ~Lab,
  "E1 — What is the partial effect?",                    "Estimate β under the model",       "by assumption (A/B/C compass)",                    "Lab 1",
  "E2 — What would change under intervention?",          "Estimate a counterfactual",        "by research design (RCT, DiD, IV, RDD, DML)",      "Lab 3"
) %>%
  gt() %>%
  tab_style(style = cell_text(weight = "bold"),
            locations = cells_column_labels()) %>%
  tab_style(style = cell_fill(color = "#fff5f5"),
            locations = cells_body(rows = 1)) %>%
  tab_style(style = cell_fill(color = "#f5e6f0"),
            locations = cells_body(rows = 2)) %>%
  tab_options(table.font.size = "13px",
              table.width = "100%",
              column_labels.font.size = "12px",
              column_labels.background.color = "#f5f5f5")
```


.pull-left[
### E1 — model given
`r fa('arrow-right', fill='#D50006')` Identification settled **before** the data, by specifying the equation.

`r fa('arrow-right', fill='#D50006')` Same path E logic students saw in Sessions 1 + 2.

`r fa('forward', fill='#D50006')` Today: **Lab 1** stress-tests E1.
]

.pull-right[
### E2 — model earns its claim
`r fa('arrow-right', fill='#7d0a52')` Identification comes from the **data structure** — randomization, parallel trends, instrument validity.

`r fa('arrow-right', fill='#7d0a52')` "Design-based identification" (Angrist &amp; Pischke 2010).

`r fa('forward', fill='#7d0a52')` Today: **Lab 3** operationalizes E2.
]

???
* E1 and E2 both live under Path E — they ask "what is" — but they differ in *what counts* as identification
* E1 is the classical econometrics curriculum; E2 is the credibility-revolution addition (Angrist/Pischke 2010)
* Path P (Prediction) sits beside them — it asks "what next?" and uses out-of-sample generalisation as its yardstick
* The labs are mapped: Lab 1 → E1 (and gateway to E2); Lab 2 → P; Lab 3 → E2


---
class: left

.blockquote[The two dangers of naive data use]

## Failed generalisation and the causality trap

When managers trust algorithmic rules blindly, they fall into one of two traps. Both are direct consequences of skipping a link in the **complexity – generalisation – causality** chain.

.pull-left[
### `r fa('triangle-exclamation', fill='#D50006')` Danger 1 — Failed induction
**The model never learnt a real rule** — only the random fluctuation of our specific sample (*overfitting*).

* **Consequence:** prediction collapses on new data — a forecast tool that works on training stores fails in new ones.
* **Mechanism:** in-sample $R^2$ is mechanically high; out-of-sample MSE is terrible.
* **Cure:** out-of-sample evaluation (train–test split, cross-validation) and regularisation. This is Lab 2.
]

.pull-right[
### `r fa('diagram-project', fill='#7d0a52')` Danger 2 — Blind deduction under intervention
**The rule is real, but only as a correlation.** A hidden confounder (e.g. school holidays) drives both $x$ and $y$.

* **Story:** *"High price ↔ high sales"* in the data, because holidays raise both demand and price. Management raises prices on a random Tuesday in November — sales collapse.
* **Mechanism:** correlation patterns break under intervention. The Lucas critique in business clothing.
* **Cure:** causal inference — experiments, IV, DiD, DML. This is Lab 3.
]

.small[**The chain matters.** A model that survives **only** Danger 1 (good cross-validation) can still fall into Danger 2 (bad causal claim). A model that survives **only** Danger 2 (clean identification) can still fall into Danger 1 (overfit confidence intervals). Real business decisions need both links — which is why the labs walk through both in turn.]

.quelle[.small[`r Citet(bib, "taddy_modern_2023")` ch. 1; Lucas (1976) on policy invariance; the causality-trap framing follows Schrage (2014, *Innovator's Hypothesis*).]]

???
* This is the conceptual slide that pre-loads the whole rest of the session
* Both dangers map directly to specific labs — students see the route
* Speaking line: "The classical OLS course teaches one of these. Modern data analytics needs both."

.blockquote[Part 2 · The A/B/C compass]

## Model Assumptions — the A/B/C compass

```{r abc-compass}
#| echo: false

tibble::tribble(
  ~Group, ~Assumption,                          ~`What we check`,                                                            ~Tool,                                                                ~`What residuals cannot tell us`,
  "A",    "A1 (variable selection)",            "OVB and overfitting are not directly testable",                            "Substantive reasoning, domain knowledge, sensitivity analysis",      "Whether the model is the 'right' one",
  "A",    "A2 (linearity)",                     "Systematic curvature in residuals vs. fitted",                             "Residuals vs. Fitted plot",                                          "—",
  "A",    "A3 (parameter constancy)",           "Influential observations that shift parameters",                           "Cook's distance, Residuals vs. Leverage",                            "Whether parameters are truly constant in the population",
  "B",    "B1 (E[ε] = 0)",                      "Automatically satisfied with intercept",                                    "(No diagnostic needed)",                                             "—",
  "B",    "B2 (homoscedasticity)",              "Non-constant residual spread",                                              "Scale-Location, Residuals vs. Fitted; Breusch-Pagan",                "—",
  "B",    "B3 (no autocorrelation)",            "Residual correlation across time or observations",                          "ACF plot, Durbin-Watson test",                                       "Non-time-based dependence (e.g. clustering)",
  "B",    "B4 (normality of errors)",           "Tail deviations in Q-Q plot",                                               "Q-Q plot, Shapiro-Wilk test",                                        "— (relevant only for small-sample inference)",
  "C",    "C1 (exogeneity)",                    "Cov(X, ε) = 0 — endogeneity not directly observable",                       "Substantive reasoning, instruments, study design",                   "Whether unobserved confounders correlate with X",
  "C",    "C2 (no perfect multicollinearity)",  "Numerical near-singularity of X'X",                                         "VIF, condition number",                                              "—"
) %>%
  gt(groupname_col = "Group", row_group_as_column = TRUE) %>%
  gt::tab_style(
    style = gt::cell_fill(color = "#FBE6E7"),
    locations = gt::cells_body(rows = Group == "A")
  ) %>%
  gt::tab_style(
    style = gt::cell_fill(color = "#F0F0F0"),
    locations = gt::cells_body(rows = Group == "B")
  ) %>%
  gt::tab_style(
    style = gt::cell_fill(color = "#EFEBF4"),
    locations = gt::cells_body(rows = Group == "C")
  ) %>%
  gt::tab_style(
    style = gt::cell_borders(sides = "bottom", color = "#686868", weight = gt::px(2)),
    locations = gt::cells_body(rows = Assumption %in% c("A3 (parameter constancy)", "B4 (normality of errors)"))
  ) %>%
  gt::tab_style(
    style = gt::cell_text(weight = "bold"),
    locations = gt::cells_row_groups()
  ) %>%
  gt::tab_style(
    style = gt::cell_fill(color = "#F5F0FA"),
    locations = gt::cells_column_labels()
  ) %>%
  gt::tab_options(table.font.size = "11px",
                  data_row.padding = px(2))
```

.quelle[.small[`r Citet(bib, "vonAuer_2023")` · Lab 1 Step 2]]

???
* Identical table to Lab 1 — students see it again for recognition
* Two empirical groups: **A** (specification) and **C1** (exogeneity) require substantive reasoning, not residual checks
* **A2, A3, B2, B3, B4, C2** can be checked from residuals; **A1, C1** cannot
* This is the diagnostic compass — what violation does which path-specific damage is on the next slide

class: left

.blockquote[Part 2 · BLUE & Bias–Variance]

## Bias vs. variance — and the BLUE property of OLS

.panelset[

.panel[.panel-name[BLUE]
### Gauss–Markov theorem

If A, B, and C assumptions hold, OLS is **BLUE**:

| | Meaning |
|:--|:----------|
| **B**est | Smallest variance among all... |
| **L**inear | ...linear... |
| **U**nbiased | ...unbiased... |
| **E**stimators | ...estimators |

`r fa('triangle-exclamation', fill='#D50006')` "Best" = **variance only**, not total error.
]

.panel[.panel-name[Trade-off]
### Bias-variance trade-off

$$\text{MSE} = \text{Bias}^2 + \text{Variance}$$

* BLUE demands: $\text{Bias} = 0$
* `r fa('arrow-right', fill='#502479')` But allowing **a little bias** can shrink the variance dramatically
* `r fa('arrow-right', fill='#D50006')` Net effect: **lower total error** on new data

`r fa('triangle-exclamation', fill='#D50006')` BLUE is theoretically elegant; in modern data settings, **not always optimal**.

In Part 3 we use the trade-off actively: *some* bias, **much** less variance → regularisation (Lasso, Ridge).
]
]



???
.small[Four shooting-target patterns. **Bias** is *how far the average shot is from the bullseye* (validity); **variance** is *how spread the shots are* (reliability). Top-left is the gold standard. Top-right is reliable but systematically wrong. Bottom-left is on target on average but useless on any single try. Bottom-right is both wrong and unreliable.]

* This three-panel slide is the deutsch "BLUE + Bias-Varianz"-Panel adapted
* Panel 1 (targets) is the visceral image; Panel 2 (BLUE) is the formal property; Panel 3 (trade-off) is the bridge to Part 3
* Speaking line: "Classical statistics asks: which estimator is BLUE? Modern data analytics asks: should I want BLUE at all?"

.quellePanURL[.small[`r Citet(bib, "taddy_modern_2023")` ch. 3; `r Citet(bib, "hastie_tibshirani_friedman_2009")` §2.9; targets visual is the classical Stocker (Innsbruck) didactic.]]

class: left

.blockquote[Part 2 · BLUE]

## What BLUE is — and what violations mean for each path

.small[Under the A/B/C assumptions, OLS is the **B**est **L**inear **U**nbiased 
**E**stimator. The same coefficient estimate $\hat{\beta}$ serves both paths — 
but a violation hits the two paths very differently:]

```{r blue-consequences, echo=FALSE}
tibble::tribble(
  ~`Violation type`,           ~Examples,          ~`Effect on the estimator`,                         ~`Path E (inference)`,                                                        ~`Path P (prediction)`,
  "Bias violations",           "A1, A2, A3, C1",   "$\\hat{\\beta}$ biased and inconsistent",          "estimates the wrong parameter — CIs and tests meaningless",                  "$\\hat{y}$ systematically wrong, but may still predict adequately if relationships stay stable (Lucas caveat)",
  "Efficiency violations",     "B2, B3, C2",       "unbiased, but inefficient",                        "SE incorrect $\\rightarrow$ CIs and tests invalid; robust / HAC SE can repair", "point predictions remain unbiased; prediction is comparatively robust",
  "Distribution violations",   "B4",               "still BLUE",                                       "exact small-sample tests invalid; large $n$ $\\rightarrow$ CLT keeps tests valid", "unaffected for point prediction"
) %>%
  gt::gt() %>%
  gt::fmt_markdown(columns = everything()) %>%
  gt::tab_style(
    style = gt::cell_fill(color = "#FBE6E7"),
    locations = gt::cells_body(rows = 1)
  ) %>%
  gt::tab_style(
    style = gt::cell_fill(color = "#F0F0F0"),

  ) %>%

    locations = gt::cells_column_labels()
  ) %>%
  gt::tab_style(
    style = gt::cell_text(weight = "bold"),
    locations = gt::cells_column_labels()
  ) %>%
  gt::tab_options(
    table.font.size = "13px",
    data_row.padding = gt::px(6)
  )
```
.center[.small[*Path E breaks under bias; Path P only breaks if the DGP changes (Lucas caveat). The next slide visualises this as the BLUE bridge.*]]

.quelle[.small[`r Citet(bib, "vonAuer_2023")` · Lab 1 Step 2 (BLUE bridge box)]]

???
* Same table as Lab 1's BLUE-bridge background box — students see the same logic in slides and lab
* **Bias violations** (A1, A2, A3, C1): break Path E entirely; Path P survives only if the DGP stays stable (Lucas caveat)
* **Efficiency violations** (B2, B3, C2): SE wrong for Path E (fix with robust / HAC SE); Path P unaffected
* **Distribution violations** (B4): no consequences for BLUE; only matters for small-n exact inference
* The β̂ symbol is replaced with "the estimator" to avoid Unicode combining-mark issues in HTML tables

class: left

.blockquote[Part 2 · The bridge]

## BLUE as the bridge between paths

```{r blue-bridge-svg}
#| echo: false
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-align: center
knitr::include_graphics(xfun::from_root("img","Session3","blue_bridge.svg"))
```

???
* BLUE is the common starting point both paths share — under assumptions A/B/C, OLS is the unbiased benchmark
* Path P branches *upward*: deliberately accept bias for variance reduction (the "bias-variance trade-off", Hastie/Tibshirani/Friedman 2009). The toolkit is Ridge / Lasso / Elastic Net + cross-validation. Lab 2 operates here.
* Path E branches *downward*: preserve unbiasedness, and add design-based identification (Angrist & Pischke 2010). The toolkit is robust SE, RCT, DiD, IV, DML. Lab 1 & Lab 3 operate here.
* The Spiess (2025) point at the bottom: preserving unbiasedness is also an *institutional* discipline — it prevents the researcher from tuning the analysis toward a favoured result. Pre-commitment makes the estimate credible.
* This is the punchline of Part 2 — every method in today's labs sits on one of these two branches

class: left

.blockquote[Part 2 · Beyond the linear model]

## From the linear model to generalised linear models

Our Sessions 1–3 framework uses **`lm()`** — the linear model. Real business questions often have outcomes that the linear model handles poorly: a customer either buys or does not (binary), a user clicks $0, 1, 2, \dots$ times (count), a contract lasts a certain number of weeks (duration). The generalised linear model (**GLM**) is the natural extension.

.pull-left[
### Linear model (LM)

$$\mathbb{E}[Y \mid X] = X\boldsymbol{\beta}$$

* $Y$ continuous
* OLS estimation
* In `r fa('r-project')`: `lm()` — what Labs 1–3 use throughout

### Generalised linear model (GLM)

$$g\bigl(\mathbb{E}[Y \mid X]\bigr) = X\boldsymbol{\beta}$$

* $g(\cdot)$ — the **link function**
* Maximum-likelihood estimation
* In `r fa('r-project')`: `glm(family = ...)`

.center[
<img src="figures/glm_venn_lazic.png" style="width:78%; margin-top:8px;"/>
]
.small[Nested model family.]
]

.pull-right[
### Why GLM matters in business

Many business outcomes are not continuous:

| Business question | $Y$ | GLM variant |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Will the customer buy? | binary | Logit |
| How many clicks? | count | Poisson |
| Time until purchase? | duration | Gamma |

### Outlook (→ ER017): logistic regression

$$P(Y\!=\!1 \mid X) = \frac{1}{1+e^{-X\boldsymbol{\beta}}}$$

`r fa('triangle-exclamation', fill='#D50006')` **In Lab 1** we already see the limit of `lm()`: when $Y$ is binary (e.g. "Did the customer redeem the coupon?"), `lm()` can produce $\hat y \notin [0,1]$ — nonsensical probabilities. `glm(family = binomial)` solves this.

ER017 will pick up the GLM-for-business toolkit systematically — logit, Poisson, survival, and their causal extensions.
]

.quelle[.small[see Introductory chapter in `r Citet(bib, "taddy_modern_2023")` for business applications.]]

???
* This slide is the "Brücke zu ER017" requested explicitly
* The Lab 1 link is honest: students will encounter the binary-outcome problem in passing, and the `glm()` resolution is signposted
* Speaking line: "Linear is enough to learn the grammar. GLM is the grammar applied to real business outcomes."

class: inverse, center, middle

# Part 3

## Brief Introduction to Machine Learning

.blockquote[*Why prediction is not estimation — and what changes.*]



---
class: left

## The in-sample illusion

When the same data fit *and* judge the model, performance is **mechanically** good. With $p$ free parameters, OLS minimises the in-sample RSS by construction. Adding any regressor — useful or not — weakly *raises* $R^2$.

.pull-left[
```{r toy-polynomial-slide, echo=FALSE, fig.width=6.6, fig.height=3.6, out.width="100%"}
set.seed(42)
n  <- 30
x  <- sort(runif(n, 0, 10))
y  <- sin(x) + rnorm(n, sd = 0.4)
xg <- seq(0, 10, length.out = 200)
m1 <- lm(y ~ x)
m3 <- lm(y ~ poly(x, 3))
mH <- lm(y ~ poly(x, 15))

par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(3.5, 3.5, 2.2, 0.5),
    mgp = c(2, 0.6, 0), cex.lab = 0.95, cex.main = 1.0)

plot(x, y, pch = 19, col = "#686868",
     main = "Underfit (degree 1)",
     xlab = "x", ylab = "y")
lines(xg, predict(m1, newdata = data.frame(x = xg)),
      col = "#D50006", lwd = 2.4)

plot(x, y, pch = 19, col = "#686868",
     main = "Good fit (degree 3)",
     xlab = "x", ylab = "y")
lines(xg, predict(m3, newdata = data.frame(x = xg)),
      col = "#502479", lwd = 2.4)

plot(x, y, pch = 19, col = "#686868",
     main = "Overfit (degree 15)",
     xlab = "x", ylab = "y", ylim = range(y) + c(-0.6, 0.6))
lines(xg, predict(mH, newdata = data.frame(x = xg)),
      col = "#7d0a52", lwd = 2.4)
```
]

.pull-right[
.small[
**Three fits of the same 30 points.**

* Degree 1: high bias, low variance — *underfits*
* Degree 3: balanced — recovers the structure
* Degree 15: low bias on training data, high variance — *memorises noise*

In-sample $R^2$ rises monotonically from left to right. Out-of-sample, the right panel collapses. This is the **central problem of prediction**: classical fit statistics are blind to it.
]
]

.quelle[.small[Toy example used here is the same as Lab 2 Step 3 — `r Citet(bib, "taddy_modern_2023")` style.]]

???
* The toy polynomial is a generic ML principle — not the actual Lab 2 result
* In Lab 2 the OJ data at $n \approx 28\,000$ is *too large* for OLS to fully break: Variant C with $p \approx 36$ still generalises
* The slide makes the principle visible at $n = 30$, $p$ up to 15 — where OLS clearly fails
* Speaking line: "Whether we hit the wall depends on $n / p$. The lesson is the *direction* of the trade-off, not a universal collapse."



---
class: left

## In-sample $R^2$ vs. out-of-sample loss

The fit statistics that look familiar from Lab 1 ($R^2$, $\hat\sigma^2$, $t$-statistics) all describe the **training fit**. They tell us how well the model recovered the sample we already saw. The honest predictive question is different: *how badly will the model do on a sample it has never seen?*

.pull-left[
The expected out-of-sample squared error of a prediction $\hat{f}(x_0)$ decomposes into three additive terms:

$$\mathbb{E}\!\bigl[(y_0 - \hat{f}(x_0))^2\bigr] = \underbrace{\mathrm{Bias}^2}_{\text{model rigidity}} + \underbrace{\mathrm{Var}}_{\text{model sensitivity}} + \underbrace{\sigma^2_\varepsilon}_{\text{irreducible}}$$

* Adding parameters lowers Bias² but raises Variance
* In-sample RSS sees only Bias² + sample noise — never the Variance term
* The minimum of the sum sits **strictly to the left of zero bias**
]

.pull-right[
.center[
<img src="figures/bias_variance_tradeoff.svg" style="width:95%;"/>
]
.small[Bias², Variance and total error as functions of model complexity. The lowest *total* error lies between the bias-minimum and the variance-minimum — never at either extreme.]
]

.quelle[.small[`r Citet(bib, "taddy_modern_2023")` ch. 1; `r Citet(bib, "hastie_tibshirani_friedman_2009")` §2.9.]]

???
* This is the key picture for the whole module — every following slide refers back to it
* Bias² and Variance are theoretical quantities; we approximate them via train/test split or CV
* Lab 2 Step 4 implements the OOS evaluation: 5-fold CV
* The irreducible $\sigma^2_\varepsilon$ remains — no model, however flexible, can predict pure noise
* Speaking line: "Lab 1 trained your eyes on Bias. Lab 2 trains them on Variance. Both matter."



---
class: left

## When more variables hurt: the curse of dimensionality

Classical statistics relies on $n \gg p$. When the candidate set of regressors $p$ grows faster than the sample $n$, four interlocked problems erode OLS performance — long before any "Big Data" regime begins.

```{r fhl-table, echo=FALSE}
tibble::tribble(
  ~Problem,                       ~`What happens`,                                       ~Consequence,
  "1. Noise accumulation",        "Each irrelevant regressor injects estimation variance.", "Predictions degrade even when no new signal is added.",
  "2. Spurious correlation",      "With many candidates, some correlate with $y$ by chance.", "Selected variables look significant — but are not.",
  "3. Incidental endogeneity",    "Random correlations between $x_j$ and $\\varepsilon$.",   "OLS becomes inconsistent: $\\hat\\beta \\not\\to \\beta$.",
  "4. Measurement error",         "Many predictors $\\Rightarrow$ many noisy variables.",    "Attenuation bias amplifies as $p$ grows."
) %>%
  gt() %>%
  tab_style(cell_fill("#f5f0fa"), cells_column_labels()) %>%
  tab_style(cell_text(weight = "bold"), cells_column_labels()) %>%
  fmt_markdown(columns = everything()) %>%
  tab_options(table.font.size = "13px",
              column_labels.font.size = "13.5px")
```

.small[Lasso addresses problems **1 and 2** directly (selection + shrinkage). Problems 3 and 4 require *design* — they are why Path E2 cannot be solved by penalisation alone, and why Lab 3 turns to DML and instrumental variables.]

.quelle[.small[`r Citet(bib, "fan_bigdata_2014")`.]]

???
* This is the diagnosis — Lasso is one response, but not the only one
* Note: incidental endogeneity is the bridge to causal inference
* For ER114, points 1–2 are the operational message; 3–4 are the theoretical caveat



---
class: left

## The naïve answer: stepwise selection

Confronted with too many variables, the classical response is **mechanical pruning**: start with all, drop the worst on AIC, repeat until removing anything makes the model worse. The procedure is computationally cheap and intuitively appealing — *and it fails on every count that matters for inference.*

.pull-left[
### `r fa('xmark', fill='#D50006')` Four reasons why stepwise selection is unreliable

1. **Automated $p$-hacking** — searching $2^p$ candidate models all but guarantees spurious "significance"
2. **Standard errors are too small** — they treat the selected variables as if known *a priori*; they are not
3. **Coefficients are biased upward** — winner's curse: surviving variables overstate their true effects
4. **Path-dependence** — removing variable $j$ rearranges the partial correlations of all others; no global optimum guaranteed
]

.pull-right[
### `r fa('arrows-rotate', fill='#502479')` What changes with penalisation?

Lasso replaces the discrete *include / exclude* choice with a continuous **shrinkage**: coefficients are pulled toward zero, and some are pulled *to* zero. The selection step and the estimation step happen jointly under a single convex loss.

This does not solve all four problems above. But it makes them **operational** — we can tune them via cross-validation rather than by hand.
]

.small[Stepwise selection survives in software because it is fast and old. It does not survive scrutiny. The classic critique by `r Citet(bib, "harrell_2015")` has been settled for two decades; modern predictive practice prefers regularisation. Lab 2 Step 4 makes the failure visible on a small-sample subset of the Dominick's data.]

???
* Reference back to Lab 2 Step 4 ("regional manager with 5 stores" demonstration)
* In Lab 2 the full-sample stepwise is computationally stable — 45 → 41 variables — but the regional subset shows the volatility
* This is the bridge: stepwise *can* work at $n \gg p$, but it is methodologically the wrong tool
* Speaking line: "Stepwise is a search for noise that happens to align with the current sample"



---
class: left

## A unified view: the penalised regression family

OLS minimises in-sample RSS unconditionally. Every member of the **penalised regression family** adds a penalty on $\boldsymbol{\beta}$ — different shapes, same intent: trade a little bias for a lot less variance.

```{r penalty-family, echo=FALSE}
tibble::tribble(
  ~Method,                       ~`Objective (minimise)`,                                                       ~`Penalty shape`,         ~`Sets coefficients = 0?`,
  "OLS",                         "$\\sum_i (y_i - x_i^\\top\\beta)^2$",                                          "—",                       "No",
  "Ridge `r fa('square')`",      "$\\sum_i (y_i - x_i^\\top\\beta)^2 + \\lambda \\sum_j \\beta_j^2$",            "$L_2$ (smooth, round)",   "No — shrinks, never zeros",
  "Lasso `r fa('diamond')`",     "$\\sum_i (y_i - x_i^\\top\\beta)^2 + \\lambda \\sum_j |\\beta_j|$",            "$L_1$ (angular, corner)", "Yes — sparse selection",
  "Elastic Net",                 "$\\text{RSS} + \\lambda\\bigl(\\alpha|\\beta|_1 + (1-\\alpha)\\beta^2\\bigr)$","Mixture",                 "Partially — keeps correlated groups"
) %>%
  gt() %>%
  tab_style(cell_fill("#f5f0fa"), cells_column_labels()) %>%
  tab_style(cell_text(weight = "bold"), cells_column_labels()) %>%
  fmt_markdown(columns = everything()) %>%
  tab_options(table.font.size = "12.5px")
```

.small[$\lambda \to 0$ recovers OLS. $\lambda \to \infty$ shrinks everything to the intercept. The tuning is **out-of-sample** — typically via $k$-fold cross-validation.]

.quelle[.small[`r Citet(bib, "tibshirani_1996")` (Lasso); Hoerl & Kennard 1970 (Ridge); Zou & Hastie 2005 (Elastic Net).]]

???
* Three methods, one frame — only the penalty geometry differs
* The Elastic Net case matters when predictors are clustered (e.g. the 11 demographics in Lab 2: income/educ/hval150 move together)
* Lasso may arbitrarily pick one from a correlated group; Elastic Net keeps groups together
* Lab 2 Bonus B1 lets students compare all three on the OJ data



---
class: left

## Why Lasso selects and Ridge shrinks: the geometry

Both penalties shrink. Only Lasso **sets coefficients exactly to zero**. The reason is geometric: the $L_1$ ball has corners on the coordinate axes; the $L_2$ ball does not.

.pull-left[
.center[
<img src="figures/l1_l2_geometry.svg" style="width:88%;"/>
]
.small[The OLS solution $\hat\beta_{OLS}$ is the centre of the elliptical RSS contours. The constrained solution is the **first contact point** between an RSS ellipse and the penalty region. For Lasso (left, diamond) this contact occurs *on an axis* — one coefficient is set to zero. For Ridge (right, circle) the contact is *generically interior* — no coefficient is zero, just smaller.]
]

.pull-right[
This is not a numerical artefact. It is a **structural property** of the $L_1$ norm:

* Lasso's penalty $|\beta_1| + |\beta_2|$ has corners
* The probability that the RSS-contour touches a corner is positive (not zero)
* As $\lambda$ rises, *more* corners are hit — more coefficients zeroed
* This is what "variable selection by Lasso" means concretely

Ridge's penalty $\beta_1^2 + \beta_2^2$ has *no* corners — its level sets are smooth circles. Contact points are generically interior. Coefficients shrink but never disappear.
]

.quelle[.small[`r Citet(bib, "tibshirani_1996")`; `r Citet(bib, "hastie_tibshirani_friedman_2009")` fig. 3.11.]]

???
* The geometry slide is purely conceptual; no code
* Students who saw this once will remember Lasso = corners forever
* If the SVG doesn't render, fall back: describe verbally, refer to Hastie et al. fig. 3.11

# Geometrische Intuition: Lasso (L₁) vs. Ridge (L₂)

## Grundprinzip: Constrained Optimization

Beide Regularisierungsmethoden lösen dasselbe Grundproblem: Minimiere die Residuenquadratsumme (RSS), aber **beschränkt auf eine Region** im Parameterraum. Die gestrichelten Ellipsen in der Abbildung sind die **Konturlinien der Verlustfunktion** — Linien gleicher RSS-Werte. Sie sind elliptisch, weil die Verlustfunktion quadratisch in \(\beta\) ist. Ihr Zentrum ist der **OLS-Schätzer** \(\hat{\beta}_{\text{OLS}}\), der die RSS ohne Restriktionen minimiert.

Die farbige Form — Raute (Lasso) bzw. Kreis (Ridge) — ist die **Constraint-Region**:

- **Lasso:** \(|\beta_1| + |\beta_2| \leq t\) → Raute (L₁-Ball)
- **Ridge:** \(\beta_1^2 + \beta_2^2 \leq t\) → Kreis (L₂-Ball)

Der regularisierte Schätzer liegt an dem Punkt, wo die **erste Konturlinie die Constraint-Region berührt** — also so nah wie möglich am OLS-Optimum, ohne die Restriktion zu verletzen. Der Radius \(t\) der Constraint-Region entspricht dem inversen Strafparameter \(\lambda\): ein kleines \(t\) (starke Regularisierung) zwingt die Lösung nah an den Ursprung.



## Lasso (L₁): Kontakt an der Ecke

Die Raute hat **Ecken auf den Koordinatenachsen**. Da die Konturellipsen in der Regel zuerst eine Ecke berühren (und nicht eine glatte Kante), landet die Lösung typischerweise genau auf einer Achse — im Bild bei \(\hat{\beta}_1 = 0\).

Das ist der geometrische Grund, warum Lasso **exakte Nullen produziert** und damit automatische Variablenselektion betreibt. Die Ecken der Raute „ziehen" die Lösung auf die Achsen. Formal entspricht das dem Lagrange-Problem:

\[ \hat{\beta}_{\text{Lasso}} = \arg\min_\beta \left[ \sum_i (y_i - x_i'\beta)^2 + \lambda \sum_j |\beta_j| \right] \]

Der L₁-Penalty ist an den Achsen **nicht differenzierbar** — genau diese Nicht-Differenzierbarkeit ist der analytische Grund für exakte Nullen (Subgradientenbedingung).



## Ridge (L₂): Kontakt im Inneren

Der Kreis hat **keine Ecken**. Die Konturlinie berührt ihn an einem glatten Punkt auf der Kreisbahn — weder auf \(\beta_1 = 0\) noch auf \(\beta_2 = 0\). Beide Koeffizienten werden **geschrumpft, aber niemals exakt auf null gesetzt**. Das Optimierungsproblem lautet:

\[ \hat{\beta}_{\text{Ridge}} = \arg\min_\beta \left[ \sum_i (y_i - x_i'\beta)^2 + \lambda \sum_j \beta_j^2 \right] \]

Ridge hat eine **geschlossene analytische Lösung**:

\[ \hat{\beta}_{\text{Ridge}} = (X'X + \lambda I)^{-1} X'y \]

Der Term \(\lambda I\) macht die Matrix \((X'X + \lambda I)\) stets invertierbar — auch bei Multikollinearität oder \(n < p\). Das ist ein numerischer Vorteil von Ridge gegenüber OLS.



## Gegenüberstellung

| Eigenschaft | Lasso (L₁) | Ridge (L₂) |
|:------------|:-----------|:-----------|
| Constraint-Region | Raute (spitze Ecken) | Kreis (glatt) |
| Kontaktpunkt | Typisch auf der Achse | Auf der Kreiskurve |
| Koeffizienten | Exakt null möglich | Nur Schrumpfung, nie null |
| Effekt | Selektion + Schrumpfung | Nur Schrumpfung |
| Analytische Lösung | Nein (iterativ, z. B. LARS) | Ja: \((X'X + \lambda I)^{-1}X'y\) |
| Vorteil bei | Sparsamen Modellen, Selektion | Multikollinearität, stabiler Schrumpfung |
| Nachteil | Wählt bei korrelierten Prädiktoren nur einen | Kein sparsames Modell |



## Elastic Net als Kompromiss

Bei korrelierten Prädiktoren (z. B. Kreuzpreise) hat Lasso eine bekannte Schwäche: Es wählt aus einer Gruppe korrelierter Variablen tendenziell nur **eine** und setzt die anderen auf null — welche, hängt von numerischen Zufälligkeiten ab. **Elastic Net** kombiniert beide Penalties:

\[ \hat{\beta}_{\text{EN}} = \arg\min_\beta \left[ \sum_i (y_i - x_i'\beta)^2 + \lambda_1 \sum_j |\beta_j| + \lambda_2 \sum_j \beta_j^2 \right] \]

Geometrisch entspricht die Constraint-Region einer **abgerundeten Raute** — sie hat Ecken (→ Selektion möglich) aber keine scharfen Kanten (→ korrelierte Variablen werden gemeinsam geschrumpft, nicht willkürlich herausselektiert).



## Bezug zum Dominick's-Lab

Im Lab mit \(p \approx 36\) `brand:demo`-Interaktionstermen ist die geometrische Logik direkt anwendbar:

- **Lasso** setzt irrelevante Terme wie `Dominick's:income` exakt auf null und liefert ein sparsiomes, interpretierbares Modell — genau das, was Sarah Chen für das Inventory-Tool braucht.
- **Ridge** würde alle 36 Terme beibehalten (nur kleiner) und die Frage „Welche Demografievariablen *wirklich* wichtig sind?" nicht beantworten.
- **Elastic Net** ist bei den Kreuzpreisen (\(\log p_{\text{MM}}\), \(\log p_{\text{TR}}\), \(\log p_{\text{Dom}}\)), die konstruktionsbedingt korreliert sind, die robustere Wahl als reines Lasso.



---
class: left

.blockquote[Regularisation in operation]

## Lasso in practice — the regularisation path

Lasso does not produce a single model. Across the grid of $\lambda$ values it produces a whole **regularisation path** — a sequence of candidate models, from $\lambda = 0$ (full OLS, all coefficients in) to $\lambda \to \infty$ (only the intercept). Cross-validation then picks the sweet spot.

.panelset[
.panel[.panel-name[Coefficient paths]
.pull-left[
```{r lasso-paths, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, fig.width=6.5, fig.height=4.0, out.width="100%"}
set.seed(42)
n <- 200; p <- 5
X <- matrix(rnorm(n*p), n, p)
colnames(X) <- c("Price", "Promo", "Quality", "Age", "Noise")
y <- 2*X[,1] - 1.5*X[,2] + 1*X[,3] + 0.3*X[,4] + 0*X[,5] + rnorm(n)
library(glmnet)
fit <- glmnet(X, y, alpha = 1)
beta_df <- as.data.frame(as.matrix(t(coef(fit)[-1,])))
beta_df$lambda <- fit$lambda
library(tidyr); library(ggplot2)
beta_long <- pivot_longer(beta_df, -lambda, names_to = "Variable", values_to = "Coefficient")
ggplot(beta_long, aes(log10(lambda), Coefficient, color = Variable)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", alpha = 0.3) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Price"="#D50006", "Promo"="#502479",
                                "Quality"="#27ae60", "Age"="#3498db",
                                "Noise"="#7d0a52")) +
  labs(x = expression(log[10](lambda)), y = "Coefficient value") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "right",
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
```
]

.pull-right[
.small[**Five candidate predictors, one of them pure noise.** As $\lambda$ increases (moving right on the x-axis):

* **Noise** is the first to be shrunk to zero — Lasso correctly identifies the irrelevant variable
* **Age** (small true effect) follows soon after
* **Quality** and **Promo** (moderate effects) survive longer
* **Price** (strongest signal) is the last to give in

The path *visualises selection in action*. Each $\lambda$ defines a different model. The job of cross-validation is to pick which one.]
]
]

.panel[.panel-name[Squelch analogy]
### $\lambda$ as the squelch knob

A **squelch** is the noise-suppression knob on a radio set. Turn it up too far and you hear nothing (signal blocked). Turn it down too far and you hear only static.

.pull-left[
* **$\lambda$ too small** → too little shrinkage, irrelevant variables stay in, model memorises noise (overfit)
* **$\lambda$ too large** → too much shrinkage, even strong signals are zeroed out (underfit)
* **$\lambda$ just right** → noise filtered, signal preserved
]

.pull-right[
This is the operational meaning of the bias–variance trade-off in regularisation. The squelch knob is the trade-off made physical: one continuous dial, one optimum.

`r fa('arrow-right', fill='#502479')` The optimum is *not* set by intuition. It is set by **cross-validation** on held-out data.
]
]

.panel[.panel-name[Decision rule]
### Which $\lambda$ to report

After cross-validation, glmnet returns two natural choices `r Citet(bib, "taddy_modern_2023")`:

* **CV-min rule** — $\hat\lambda$ that minimises the CV error. **Focus: predictive accuracy.** When forecast quality is the deliverable, this is the default.
* **1-SE rule** — the *largest* $\hat\lambda$ within one standard error of the minimum. **Focus: parsimony.** A more conservative, more interpretable model with fewer non-zero coefficients. For executive communication and model deployment, this is often the better choice.

.small[**Practical rule of thumb.** If the audience is a board of directors, lean 1-SE. If the audience is another statistician evaluating predictive performance, lean min. The choice should be deliberate, not accidental.]
]
]

.quelle[.small[`r Citet(bib, "tibshirani_1996")`; `r Citet(bib, "taddy_modern_2023")` ch. 3 on the 1-SE rule.]]

???
* The three-panel structure mirrors the deutsche "Synthese: CV + Lasso" — three windows on the same process
* Panel 1 visualises *what* happens; Panel 2 explains *why*; Panel 3 governs *how to report*
* Sarah's T7 memo deliberately invokes the 1-SE rule for the parsimony argument
* Speaking line: "Lasso gives you the menu. Cross-validation orders for you. Your job is to know which menu you ordered from."



---
class: left

.blockquote[Tuning $\lambda$ out-of-sample]

## How $\lambda$ is chosen: cross-validation

The penalty parameter $\lambda$ controls the bias–variance trade-off. There is no theoretical formula for the right value — it must be tuned **out of sample**. Two related instruments do the job.

.panelset[
.panel[.panel-name[Train–Test split]
.pull-left[
### The simplest version
Hold out a random 20% of the data as **test set**. Fit on the 80%. Evaluate on the 20%.

* Diagnostic: Train-MSE $\ll$ Test-MSE? → overfit.
* Reported metrics: RMSE, AUC, accuracy — *always* on the test set.
* Single split → single number. Quick, but the choice of the 20% can sway the answer.

`r fa('triangle-exclamation', fill='#D50006')` **Do not look at the test set during model selection.** If you tune anything based on test performance, that 20% becomes a *second training set* — and you lose the validity of the out-of-sample claim.
]

.pull-right[
.center[
<img src="figures/train_test_split.svg" style="width:96%;"/>
]
]
]

.panel[.panel-name[k-Fold CV]
.pull-left[
### Systematic, repeated splitting and testing

1. Partition the data into $k$ equal folds (typically $k=5$ or $10$).
2. For each candidate $\lambda$ on a grid:
   - For $j = 1, \dots, k$: fit on all folds except $j$, predict on fold $j$
   - Average the squared prediction error across folds → $\text{CV}(\lambda)$
3. Every observation is in the test set exactly once — no data leakage.

`r fa('arrow-right', fill='#502479')` More stable than a single split, especially when $n$ is moderate.
]

.pull-right[
.center[
<img src="figures/kfold_crossvalidation.svg" style="width:100%;"/>
]
]
]

.panel[.panel-name[Sweet spot]
.pull-left[
### Choosing $\hat\lambda$ from the CV curve

The CV curve is U-shaped. Two natural choices:

* **CV-min rule** — $\lambda_{\min}$ minimises CV error. Focus: maximum predictive accuracy.
* **1-SE rule** — $\lambda_{1\text{SE}}$ is the *largest* $\lambda$ within one SE of the minimum. Focus: parsimony, executive-communication-friendly, robust to CV noise.

`r fa('arrow-right', fill='#502479')` Lab 2 Step 5 uses both — most business deliverables (Sarah's memo) lean on the 1-SE choice.
]

.pull-right[
.center[
<img src="figures/cv_curve_schematic.svg" style="width:96%;"/>
]
]
]
]

.small[**One assumption worth flagging:** CV assumes folds are *exchangeable*. With panel data — like the OJ data — observations within a store are correlated, so plain random CV underestimates true OOS error. Lab 2 uses store-clustered CV. We return to this in Lab 3.]

.quelle[.small[Hastie, Tibshirani, Friedman 2009 ch. 7; Lab 2 Step 5 (CV with `cv.glmnet`).]]

???
* Three panels = three levels of sophistication, in order: 80/20 → k-fold → 1-SE rule
* Train-test-split SVG is the visual primer; k-fold grid is the upgrade; CV curve is the operational object
* Speaking line: "Never report a number on data you have looked at before."
* Clustered CV: store-level holdout, not row-level — the methodologically honest version
* The "exchangeability" caveat is the Lab-3-bridge: when data has structure, plain CV lies
