# Part 4

## Brief Introduction to Causal Inference

.blockquote[*Three questions our DGP cannot answer — and how design changes that.*]



---
class: left

.blockquote[Business motivation for causal inference]

## Why experiments matter — Schrage's Innovator's Hypothesis

Before the Pearl ladder and the DAG vocabulary, one *business* observation sets the stage. Why do high-performing data-driven firms run so many experiments?

.pull-left[
### `r fa('chart-column', fill='#D50006')` The sobering empirical reality

Microsoft's Ronny Kohavi shows real A/B-test results to expert audiences — the audience guesses the winner before the data is shown:

> *No consensus. Ever.*

* Kaushik: *"80% of the time we are wrong"*
* Kohavi: only about **⅓** of tested ideas actually improve the target metric
* Hadiaris: 5-year hit rate ≈ **33%**

> *"We are poor at assessing the value of ideas."*

.small[Conviction is not evidence. Experts systematically overestimate their own forecasts — Kahneman, Tetlock, and an entire literature on judgemental forecasting agree on this point.]
]

.pull-right[
### `r fa('flask', fill='#7d0a52')` Schrage's central thesis

> *"They run experiments not because they can confidently predict outcomes — but precisely because they can't."*

### Big Data + Little Experiments

* **Big Data** — patterns and correlations (Path P)
* **Experiments** — causal evidence (Path E2)
* **Together** — *"virtuous cycles of profitable insight"*

### Connection to today

* Sessions 1–2: *p*-hacking and HARKing → commit to the hypothesis **before** seeing the data
* Today: causal designs **operationalise** that commitment
* **Mindset for the Translator:** *Data trumps intuition — but with humility.*
]

.small[The AI Value Creator uses Big Data to generate hypotheses but is humble enough to subject those hypotheses to small, hard causal tests *before* committing budget. Part 4 of today's session is the operational toolkit for doing that.]

.quelle[.small[Schrage (2014), *The Innovator's Hypothesis*; Kohavi, Tang & Xu (2020) on industrial A/B-testing practice.]]

???
* This is the business-anchor slide that motivates the entire causal-inference part
* Without this slide, Pearl's Ladder reads as philosophy; with this slide, it reads as a *business necessity*
* Speaking line: "If experts could predict outcomes, we would not need experiments. The fact that they cannot is the entire reason this lab exists."
* The 33% hit rate is the most powerful number to lead with — it is concrete, sourced, and frightening to anyone who has ever sat in a strategy meeting



---
class: left

## From prediction to intervention — Pearl's Ladder of Causation

A predictive model answers **observational** questions: *given the patterns I have seen, what is the most likely value of $y$ when I observe $x$?* It does **not** answer interventional or counterfactual questions. The distinction is structural, not statistical — `r Citet(bib, "pearl_2009")` formalises it as three rungs.

.pull-left[
### `r fa('layer-group', fill='#7d0a52')` Three rungs

**Rung 1 — Association** *"What is?"*
$P(y \mid x)$ — the conditional distribution
*Tools:* OLS, ML, Lasso, all of Lab 1 + 2

**Rung 2 — Intervention** *"What if I do?"*
$P(y \mid \text{do}(x))$ — the post-intervention distribution
*Tools:* RCTs, A/B-tests, DiD, IV, DML

**Rung 3 — Counterfactual** *"What if I had?"*
$P(y_{x} \mid x',y')$ — for the same unit
*Tools:* structural models, mediation analysis
]

.pull-right[
.center[
<img src="figures/pearl_ladder.svg" style="width:88%;"/>
]
.small[A model fit on Rung 1 cannot generally be lifted to Rung 2 without additional assumptions. Most of statistics lives on Rung 1; most of business decision-making *needs* Rung 2.]
]

.small[Lab 1 + Lab 2 operate on **Rung 1**. Lab 3 climbs to **Rung 2**. The transition is not a refinement — it is a different question that requires different machinery.]

.quelle[.small[`r Citet(bib, "pearl_2009")` ch. 1; Pearl & Mackenzie 2018; for an accessible introduction `r Citet(bib, "huntington-klein_effect_2025")`, ch. 5.]]

???
* The Ladder is the conceptual organiser for the whole Part 4
* Rung 1 → Rung 2 is the cliff that classical econometrics didactically often glosses over
* Sarah's Q1 (does feat *cause* sales?) is a Rung 2 question — pretending Rung 1 answers it is the most common applied mistake



---
class: left

## Two fundamental problems

Climbing to Rung 2 is hard because of two deep structural obstacles. They are not estimation problems — they are problems of *what the data can possibly tell us*.

.pull-left[
### `r fa('xmark', fill='#D50006')` Holland (1986): the missing counterfactual

For each unit $i$ we observe **either** $y_i(1)$ (treated) **or** $y_i(0)$ (untreated) — never both. The individual causal effect $\tau_i = y_i(1) - y_i(0)$ is **fundamentally unobservable**.

The best we can hope for is the **average** effect $\tau = \mathbb{E}[y(1) - y(0)]$ — and even that requires a strong assumption: that **treated and untreated units would have behaved identically in the counterfactual**.

This is what RCTs deliver by construction (randomisation makes the two groups exchangeable in expectation).
]

.pull-right[
### `r fa('diagram-project', fill='#502479')` Pearl: confounding

Even with infinite data, a hidden common cause $u$ of both $x$ and $y$ produces a non-zero association that **is not** causal.

.center[
<img src="figures/dag_confounder_minimal.svg" style="width:75%;"/>
]
$$\mathrm{Cov}(x, y) \neq 0 \;\not\Rightarrow\; x \to y$$

The fix is *not* statistical (more data, better SE). The fix is **design** — either block the back-door path through $u$, or break the dependency by intervention.
]

.quelle[.small[`r Citet(bib, "holland_1986")`; `r Citet(bib, "pearl_2009")`; `r Citet(bib, "imbens_rubin_2015")` ch. 1.]]

???
* Holland (1986) is the canonical citation — the "Fundamental Problem of Causal Inference"
* Pearl's confounding frame complements it: even with the counterfactual problem solved (by averaging), confounding remains a separate obstacle
* The two problems are independent — RCTs solve both at once; observational design solves only the second (and only partially)



---
class: left

## Three sources of endogeneity — and why DGP perspective matters

For OLS, all three problems collapse into one symptom: $\mathrm{Cov}(x, \varepsilon) \neq 0$. But the **diagnosis** differs — and so do the appropriate fixes.

```{r endogeneity-trio, echo=FALSE}
tibble::tribble(
  ~Source,                   ~`Mechanism in the DGP`,                                                    ~Example,                                                       ~`Typical fix`,
  "1. Omitted-variable bias", "A relevant $z$ is correlated with both $x$ and $y$ and is left out.",       "Advertising and deals are bundled in Lab 1 — feat × deal collinearity.", "FE, IV, controls",
  "2. Simultaneity",         "$x$ and $y$ are jointly determined by feedback in the same period.",        "Manager sets price *because* she expects sales — reverse causality.",   "IV, simultaneous equations",
  "3. Measurement error",    "$x$ is observed with random noise.",                                        "Self-reported advertising spending.",                                  "IV (rare), better data",
  "4. Selection on the unobserved", "Whether unit $i$ is observed or treated depends on $\\varepsilon_i$.", "Stores enter promotions only when manager expects strong response.",   "Heckman correction, design"
) %>%
  gt() %>%
  tab_style(cell_fill("#f5f0fa"), cells_column_labels()) %>%
  tab_style(cell_text(weight = "bold"), cells_column_labels()) %>%
  fmt_markdown(columns = everything()) %>%
  tab_options(table.font.size = "12px")
```

.small[**Source 4 — selection — is special.** It is not a deficiency in our equation; it is a deficiency in our *sample*. The observed $(x_i, y_i)$ pairs are not random draws from the DGP. They are the **outcome of unit-level choices** made on the basis of unobserved expectations. In the OJ data, observed (price, sales) pairs reflect the manager's prior beliefs about demand — the data is *self-selected* into existence.]

.quelle[.small[Wooldridge 2010 §6.1–6.3; Heckman 1979; `r Citet(bib, "huntington-klein_effect_2025")` ch. 8.]]

???
* The 4-row table extends the standard Wooldridge trio with Heckman's selection — explicitly requested
* The DGP framing: selection is upstream of the equation — it determines which data we even get to see
* For the OJ data: managers run promotions strategically, prices reflect expected sales — observed variation is endogenous *by design*



---
class: left

## DAG basics: backdoor, frontdoor, collider

Three patterns explain almost every causal-identification problem. They are visible — and operational — in directed acyclic graphs (DAGs).

.center[
<img src="figures/dag_three_patterns.svg" style="width:95%;"/>
]

<div style="display:flex; gap:18px; margin-top:10px;">

<div style="flex:1; font-size:0.82em; line-height:1.45;">
<strong style="color:#D50006;">`r fa('door-open', fill='#D50006')` Backdoor</strong><br>
A path $x \leftarrow u \to y$ creates spurious association. <strong>Block</strong> by conditioning on $u$ (if observable) or by IV (if not).
</div>

<div style="flex:1; font-size:0.82em; line-height:1.45;">
<strong style="color:#502479;">`r fa('compass-drafting', fill='#502479')` Frontdoor</strong><br>
A <em>mediator</em> $m$ between $x$ and $y$ can identify the effect even when $u$ confounds the direct path. Rare in practice but theoretically central.
</div>

<div style="flex:1; font-size:0.82em; line-height:1.45;">
<strong style="color:#7d0a52;">`r fa('triangle-exclamation', fill='#7d0a52')` Collider</strong><br>
$x \to c \leftarrow y$. <strong>Conditioning on $c$ creates</strong> spurious association — even between independent causes. Never control for a collider.
</div>

</div>

.small[The collider rule is the most-violated principle in applied work: well-meaning analysts often "control for everything" — and accidentally open spurious paths instead of closing them. The DAG is the discipline that makes this visible *before* estimation.]

.quelle[.small[`r Citet(bib, "pearl_2009")` ch. 3; `r Citet(bib, "cunningham_2021")` ch. 3; `r Citet(bib, "huntington-klein_effect_2025")` ch. 7.]]

???
* The three patterns are the operational vocabulary for the rest of Part 4
* Backdoor → IV, FE, DiD (different ways to close it)
* Collider → reminds students that "more controls is better" is *false*
* For Lab 3: ShelveLoc is a candidate collider — including it can bias the price elasticity



---
class: left

## A systematic taxonomy of causal study designs

The applied literature uses two cross-cutting axes to classify study designs: **manipulation** (does the analyst set $x$?) and **setting** (laboratory, field, or natural environment?). The combination gives six cells — and almost every method in use occupies one of them.

```{r design-taxonomy, echo=FALSE}
tibble::tribble(
  ~`  `,             ~Lab,                                          ~Field,                                                       ~`Natural`,
  "**Manipulated**",     "Lab experiment; Vignette experiment",         "RCT; A/B-test; Audit study (correspondence test)",           "(rare; cf. policy pilots)",
  "**Not manipulated**", "—",                                            "—",                                                          "Natural experiment; RDD; DiD; IV"
) %>%
  gt() %>%
  tab_style(cell_fill("#f5f0fa"), cells_column_labels()) %>%
  tab_style(cell_fill("#fff8e1"), cells_body(columns = `  `)) %>%
  tab_style(cell_text(weight = "bold"), cells_column_labels()) %>%
  fmt_markdown(columns = everything()) %>%
  tab_options(table.font.size = "12.5px",
              column_labels.font.size = "13px")
```

.small[**Reading the cells.** Top-left and top-mid cells solve confounding *by construction* (randomised $x$). Top-right is rare — naturally manipulated outcomes are unusual. The bottom row contains methods that **borrow** randomness from natural variation: a policy change for DiD, a cutoff for RDD, an instrument for IV. Each method is a different answer to: *where does the as-good-as-random variation come from?*]

.quelle[.small[Harrison & List 2004; `r Citet(bib, "angrist_pischke_2009")` ch. 1; `r Citet(bib, "cunningham_2021")` ch. 4. For an introductory tour `r Citet(bib, "huntington-klein_effect_2025")` ch. 10–18.]]

???
* This is the orientation slide — students can locate every method on this 2×3 grid
* The crucial conceptual move is the bottom row: "borrowed randomness"
* DiD, RDD, IV all answer the same meta-question: *what makes part of the variation in $x$ effectively random?*
* The IAB study (next slides) sits in the top-mid cell as Vignette-in-field-survey hybrid



---
class: left

## Identification through design

`r Citet(bib, "angrist_pischke_2009")` reframe causal inference around the question: *where does the variation in $x$ come from?* Three sources, three credibility regimes.

.pull-left[
### `r fa('1', fill='#D50006')` Experimental variation
$x$ is **assigned** by the researcher — coin flip, RCT, A/B-test, audit study. The variation in $x$ is *by construction* independent of unobservables.

**Credibility:** maximal. **Cost:** high. **Coverage:** narrow (specific population, specific intervention).

### `r fa('2', fill='#502479')` Quasi-experimental variation
$x$ varies *as if randomly* due to a feature of the world: a policy threshold (RDD), a policy change (DiD), an instrument (IV).

**Credibility:** depends on the credibility of the **identification assumption** (parallel trends, exclusion restriction, monotonicity).
]

.pull-right[
### `r fa('3', fill='#7d0a52')` Observational with conditioning
$x$ varies for endogenous reasons. We hope to **block** confounding paths by conditioning on observed controls.

**Credibility:** lowest — requires *all* confounders observed, and a correctly specified DAG.

### What changes the credibility?
Across the three regimes, the **same statistical machinery** (regression, ML) can be used. What changes is the **assumption set under which the estimate has a causal interpretation**. Stronger design → weaker required assumptions.

This is the credibility revolution `r Citet(bib, "angrist_pischke_2009")` — and it is *design*, not statistics, that does the work.
]

.quelle[.small[`r Citet(bib, "angrist_pischke_2009")` ch. 1; `r Citet(bib, "cunningham_2021")` ch. 4; `r Citet(bib, "athey_imbens_2019")` for the ML-econometrics interface.]]

???
* This is the most important conceptual slide of Part 4
* The same OLS can be a Path-E estimate or a Path-P prediction — the *interpretation* depends entirely on the design
* The lab-3 examples (DiD, IV, DML) all fit cell 2 of this 3-cell taxonomy



---
class: left

## A spectrum of validity: Vignette — Audit — A/B-test

When the manipulated variable is *information presented to a decision-maker*, three closely related designs sit on a spectrum from highest *internal* to highest *external* validity.

```{r validity-spectrum, echo=FALSE}
tibble::tribble(
  ~Design,                          ~`Setting`,                          ~`What is measured`,                            ~`Internal validity`,                                       ~`External validity`,
  "**Vignette experiment**",        "Lab / online survey",                "Stated behavioural intention",                  "Very high — full control over scenario",                   "Moderate — hypothetical, social-desirability bias",
  "**Audit / correspondence study**", "Real field, fictitious profiles",   "Real decisions on fictitious applications",     "Very high — randomised profile features",                  "Very high — real decision-makers, real context",
  "**A/B-test**",                   "Real field, real users",             "Real behaviour",                                "Very high — random user assignment",                       "Very high — but typically narrow (one design element)"
) %>%
  gt() %>%
  tab_style(cell_fill("#f5f0fa"), cells_column_labels()) %>%
  tab_style(cell_text(weight = "bold"), cells_column_labels()) %>%
  fmt_markdown(columns = everything()) %>%
  tab_options(table.font.size = "11.5px")
```

.small[**Trade-offs read across the table.** Vignette is the easiest to run (no ethics committee for deception, no platform access) but measures *intentions*, not *actions*. Audit studies pay the ethical cost of deception to gain ecological validity. A/B-tests have the highest external validity but typically test only narrow design elements.]

.small[**Audit studies are field-RCTs** — methodologically a special case of the A/B-test, but with a factorial design and theory-driven hypothesis rather than commercial optimisation. The Vignette-in-the-field design is *the* canonical tool of discrimination research.]

???
* This is the cleanest 3-method comparison — each method is *both* internal- and external-valid; the difference is what they measure
* Speaking line: "If you want to know what people *say* they'd do, run a vignette. If you want to know what they *do*, run an audit. If you want to know what *works on your platform*, run an A/B test."
* IAB study (next slides) is the Vignette case — with a clever validity check (list experiment)



---
class: left

## The IAB study: a vignette experiment with a built-in validity check

The IAB study *"Immigrants' recruitment chances in the German labor market"* (2025) is a large-scale **survey experiment** embedded in the IAB Job Vacancy Survey. About 5,000 real HR decision-makers were shown hypothetical CVs whose features (origin, religion, gender, language skills, experience) were randomised. They rated on a 1–10 scale how likely they would be to invite each candidate.

.pull-left[
### `r fa('flask', fill='#502479')` Design

* **Vignette, not audit:** firms knew they were participating in a study; CVs were hypothetical (*"Imagine you receive the following application..."*)
* **Factorial randomisation** of all CV features → high internal validity
* **Real decision-makers** in their domain → reasonable external validity for HR judgements
* **Outcome:** stated hiring intention (Rung 2-attempt via Rung 1 instrument)
]

.pull-right[
### `r fa('triangle-exclamation', fill='#D50006')` Threat: social desirability

In an explicit-question format, HR managers might *say* they would treat Muslim or refugee applicants equally even if they would not. The vignette format does not eliminate this — respondents still know they are observed.

The IAB authors anticipated this and added a **list experiment** in parallel.
]

.small[Why this design matters for ER114: vignette experiments are *replicable in a Master's thesis* — no ethics-committee deception, no platform access — and they allow **theory-driven factorial designs** beyond what most A/B-tests cover.]

.quelle[.small[IAB Forschungsbericht 06/2025, [doku.iab.de/forschungsbericht/2025/fb0625.pdf](https://doku.iab.de/forschungsbericht/2025/fb0625.pdf).]]

???
* The IAB study is *intentionally chosen* as a methodologically rich example
* Contrast with the OJ data: OJ is observational with embedded RCTs; IAB is a clean survey experiment
* For a Masters thesis: replicable design, modest cost, methodologically defensible



---
class: left

## Triangulation: when two methods agree, validity rises

The clever methodological move in the IAB study is the **list experiment** run in parallel. In a list experiment, respondents do not state a sensitive answer directly — they state only *how many* of several items apply. The sensitive item is masked by the count.

.pull-left[
### `r fa('list-check', fill='#502479')` The list-experiment logic

**Treatment group** sees four items including *"I would hire a Muslim applicant"*.
**Control group** sees only the three innocuous items.

The difference in *average counts* identifies the share who would hire — without ever asking directly. Social desirability cannot operate on a count.
]

.pull-right[
### `r fa('check-double', fill='#D50006')` The triangulation argument

The vignette experiment and the list experiment are **methodologically independent**: different probabilistic structures, different cognitive load on respondents, different biases.

When *both* yield the same finding (discrimination against Muslims, refugees, and visible religious symbols), the joint inference is **far stronger** than either alone — because two unrelated paths of error would have to coincidentally produce the same result.

This is the operational meaning of *validity-by-triangulation* — and it generalises well beyond the IAB context.
]

.small[**A general lesson.** Single-method studies — however well-executed — are vulnerable to method-specific bias. Triangulation through *different* methodological lenses on the *same* question is the most reliable defence. Lab 3 will return to this with the DiD–IV–DML triangulation.]

.quelle[.small[IAB 06/2025; Glynn 2013 (list experiments); Imbens 2010 on triangulation in design-based inference.]]

???
* Triangulation is the conceptual high point of Part 4
* It connects causal inference (which design?) to scientific epistemology (which inference is credible?)
* This is also where Spiess (2025) institutional argument resonates: pre-commitment + multi-method = credibility



---
class: left

## A note on our own data: Dominick's contains embedded RCTs

A footnote worth making explicit before Lab 3. The KiltsCenter documentation states:

> *"From 1989 to 1994, the University of Chicago Booth School of Business and Dominick's Finer Foods entered into a partnership for store-level research into shelf management and pricing. Together, they conducted **randomized experiments in more than 25 different categories** throughout all stores in this 100-store chain."* — KiltsCenter Marketing Database documentation

.pull-left[
### What this means

The Dominick's data is **not** purely observational. Parts of the price and shelf-position variation across stores and weeks are the result of **deliberate randomisation** by the Chicago/DFF research team.

For Labs 1 and 2 we treated the data as observational — this is a **didactic simplification**. The methodological story is more layered:

* Some weeks have experimentally-randomised prices → clean Rung-2 variation
* Other weeks have manager-set prices → endogenous Rung-1 variation
* The data **mixes both** in the panel
]

.pull-right[
### Why we mention it here

The applied lesson generalises: **real datasets often contain experimental islands within observational seas.** Identifying the islands turns a passive analysis into a quasi-experimental one.

In Lab 3 we will return to the OJ data and ask: *which sub-sample carries experimental price variation?* If we can isolate it, we can estimate the price elasticity on Rung 2 — Sarah's Q1 — without needing IV or DML.

This is not a defect of the data. It is an *opportunity* — and a model for what to look for in any business dataset.
]

.quelle[.small[`r Citet(bib, "KiltsCenter_2018")`, *Dominick's Data Manual*; available at chicagobooth.edu/research/kilts/research-data/dominicks.]]

???
* This slide is methodologically important and didactically rare
* It acknowledges the simplification of Labs 1–2 transparently
* It sets up Lab 3 as not just "more methods" but "different reading of the same data"



---
class: left

## DiD and event studies — the workhorses of design-based inference

When randomisation is not available but a **policy change** is, Difference-in-Differences (DiD) compares before-after changes between treated and untreated units. The identification assumption is **parallel trends**: absent the intervention, treated and untreated units would have followed parallel paths.

.pull-left[
### `r fa('chart-line', fill='#D50006')` Classical 2x2 DiD

For two groups (treated $T=1$, control $T=0$) and two periods (before $t=0$, after $t=1$):

$$\hat\tau_{DiD} = \bigl(\bar{y}_{T=1,t=1} - \bar{y}_{T=1,t=0}\bigr) - \bigl(\bar{y}_{T=0,t=1} - \bar{y}_{T=0,t=0}\bigr)$$

**Key assumption:** parallel trends — not testable directly, only by pre-treatment placebo tests.
]

.pull-right[
### `r fa('chart-bar', fill='#502479')` Event studies and modern DiD

Modern DiD generalises 2x2 to *staggered* adoption (units treated at different times) and *heterogeneous* effects. Naive two-way fixed-effects estimators can be **severely biased** in this setting — see `r Citet(bib, "borusyak_etal_2024")`.

Robust alternatives: imputation estimators (Borusyak et al.), Callaway–Sant'Anna 2021, Sun–Abraham 2021. Lab 3 will implement one of these on the OJ data.
]

.small[**Why this matters for Sarah's Q1.** If Dominick's ran a pricing RCT in some weeks but not others, the difference-in-differences between treated and untreated weeks isolates the causal price effect — under parallel trends. This is exactly the design opportunity hinted at on the previous slide.]

???
* DiD is the bread-and-butter of modern applied econometrics
* The Borusyak warning matters: students should know that the classical TWFE estimator is *not* the right tool for staggered adoption
* The OJ data may support a clean DiD if the experimental weeks can be identified



---
class: left

.blockquote[Borrowed randomness, continued]

## Instrumental variables and regression discontinuity

Two more design-based tools complete the toolkit for situations where a clean A/B-test is not feasible — for ethical, legal, technical, or budgetary reasons.

.pull-left[
### `r fa('shuffle', fill='#502479')` Instrumental Variables (IV / 2SLS)

**Scenario — "intent-to-treat":** We randomly assign access to a new feature (e.g. a smart-thermostat trial), but not every assigned customer actually uses it. Adoption is correlated with unobservables (tech affinity, income).

**Method:** Use the *random assignment* as an **instrument** $Z$. The first stage isolates the part of the treatment $X$ that is uncorrelated with the error; the second stage estimates the causal effect using only that exogenous part.

**Two requirements:**
* **Relevance** — $Z$ predicts $X$
* **Exclusion** — $Z$ affects $Y$ *only* through $X$, not directly

`r fa('triangle-exclamation', fill='#D50006')` Exclusion is untestable. It must be argued substantively — and is usually the weakest link.
]

.pull-right[
### `r fa('ruler-horizontal', fill='#7d0a52')` Regression Discontinuity (RDD)

**Scenario:** A treatment activates at a sharp threshold — a bonus at €100,000 annual revenue, a subsidy at age 65, a scholarship at a test-score cutoff.

**Method:** Compare units *just below* and *just above* the threshold. They are nearly identical on observable and unobservable characteristics — except for treatment. The threshold becomes a local randomisation device.

**Two requirements:**
* **Manipulation must not be possible** around the cutoff
* **The outcome must be smooth** in the running variable absent treatment

`r fa('triangle-exclamation', fill='#502479')` RDD identifies a **local** effect — only around the cutoff. External validity to other parts of the distribution is a separate question.

*(For panel data, FE and RE methods complement these tools by removing time-invariant unobserved heterogeneity.)*
]

.small[**The pattern across IV, DiD, and RDD is the same.** Each method asks: *where in the data does the variation in treatment resemble a coin flip?* That sub-variation is then used to identify the causal effect, while the rest of the data is set aside. This is why `r Citet(bib, "angrist_pischke_2009")` call applied causal econometrics *design-based*: the credibility lives in the source of variation, not in the regression that follows.]

.quelle[.small[`r Citet(bib, "angrist_pischke_2009")` ch. 4 (IV) and ch. 6 (RDD); `r Citet(bib, "cunningham_2021")` ch. 7 (IV), ch. 6 (RDD); `r Citet(bib, "huntington-klein_effect_2025")` ch. 19–20.]]

???
* This slide closes the design-based-inference triangle: DiD (previous slide) + IV + RDD
* Each method gets the same template: scenario, method, two requirements, one warning
* For Lab 3: IV is the candidate method if experimental weeks in the OJ data cannot be cleanly identified — supply-side cost shocks (wholesale-price changes) could serve as instruments
* Speaking line: "Three methods, one philosophy: find where treatment looks random, even if the rest of the data does not."



---
class: left

## When designs converge: ML meets causal inference

The traditional contrast — *ML predicts, econometrics identifies* — has been eroded over the past decade. Two literatures push the methods together.

.pull-left[
### `r fa('robot', fill='#502479')` ML for prediction *within* causal estimation
`r Citet(bib, "chernozhukov_DoubleML_2018")`'s Double Machine Learning uses ML to flexibly estimate the **nuisance functions** (the relationship between $x$ and $u$, and between $y$ and $u$) inside a causal moment condition. The causal parameter itself is estimated by orthogonal scoring — preserving valid inference even with ML in the pipeline.

`r Citet(bib, "athey_imbens_2019")` survey the rapidly growing intersection: causal forests, generalised random forests, post-double-selection Lasso.
]

.pull-right[
### `r fa('scale-balanced', fill='#D50006')` The Spiess credibility argument
`r Citet(bib, "spiess_optimalEstimation_2025")` reframes the bias–variance trade-off as an *institutional* trade-off. Pre-committing to a less flexible procedure — fewer free parameters, fewer choices made after seeing the data — buys **credibility**.

In this reading, ML is not a free lunch. The flexibility comes at the cost of researcher degrees of freedom — and these reduce the credibility of any claim about $\beta$.

Sample-splitting (used in DML) is the operational answer: separate the data into nuisance-fit and causal-estimation halves.
]

.small[`r Citet(bib, "mullainathan_MLApplied_2017")` make the simplest version of the case: *ML and econometrics ask different questions, but they share the same operating manual on bias and variance.* The convergence is conceptual before it is technical.]

???
* This is the integrative slide — Spiess + Chernozhukov + Mullainathan-Spiess in one
* The institutional argument matters: it explains why ML alone does not solve causal identification
* DML is the technical synthesis — but the *intellectual* synthesis is Spiess's

## What we learned in Lab 3

.pull-left[
### `r fa('check-double', fill='#7d0a52')` What design buys
* The same OLS, under three different designs, gives three different causal interpretations
* Within-transformation removes time-invariant store confounding — but not all endogeneity
* IV exploits supply-side cost shocks as an exclusion restriction — valid only if the instrument is uncorrelated with demand shocks
* DML preserves valid inference under flexible nuisance estimation — at the cost of needing larger samples
]

.pull-right[
### `r fa('triangle-exclamation', fill='#686868')` Where assumptions live
* Every causal estimate **rests on at least one untestable assumption** — parallel trends, exclusion, conditional ignorability
* The role of the analyst is to make the assumption **transparent and challengeable** — not to hide it under the estimate
* Lab 3 produces *three* estimates for Sarah's Q1. **Convergence across them strengthens the inference; divergence demands explanation.**
* This is what triangulation looks like in practice.
]

## The two demands of modern econometrics

The arc of this session can be summarised in one tension and one resolution.

.pull-left[
### `r fa('arrows-up-down', fill='#D50006')` The tension

**Prediction** rewards *flexibility* — more parameters, more interactions, more data-driven model choice.

**Inference** rewards *parsimony* — fewer choices made after seeing the data, fewer free parameters, more pre-commitment.

Naïvely, these pull in opposite directions. The Bias-Variance frame from Part 3 makes them *appear* to be the same trade-off — but they live on different axes.
]

.pull-right[
### `r fa('compass-drafting', fill='#502479')` The resolution

The frame that holds them together is **design**:

* On Rung 1, more data and more flexibility help — Lab 2's lesson
* On Rung 2, more *design* helps — Lab 3's lesson
* The two are not substitutes; they are complements
* The same dataset can support both — *if* we recognise where the variation came from

`r Citet(bib, "spiess_optimalEstimation_2025")`: pre-commitment is the bridge. *What we hold fixed before seeing the data* defines the credibility of what we estimate after.
]

???
* This is the synthesis slide — Part 3 + Part 4 in one frame
* Speaking line: "The same OLS line can be a forecast or a causal estimate. The difference is the design behind it, not the math in front of it."

## Looking ahead — from this Bridge Module to ER017

This session closed the Bridge Module's **first arc**: Gauss-Markov diagnostics → predictive modelling → causal inference. The methodological vocabulary you now command is the **input layer** for ER017 (*Advanced Quantitative Methods*) and the applied research projects that follow.

.pull-left[
### What ER017 will build on
* Panel methods at scale — within, between, random-effects, mixed models
* Modern DiD estimators — staggered adoption, heterogeneous effects (Borusyak, Callaway-Sant'Anna)
* Instrumental variables in practice — finding instruments, testing exclusion
* Double Machine Learning at production scale — including high-dimensional confounding
* Bayesian alternatives to frequentist identification
]

.pull-right[
### What you should be able to do now
* Read a published study and identify *which rung* of the ladder it claims to operate on
* Spot the difference between an out-of-sample claim and a causal claim
* Recognise when a control is a *confounder*, a *collider*, or a *mediator*
* Articulate the identification assumption behind any reported causal estimate
* Write the executive-level memo (Lab T7 / T_final) — the most professionally valuable skill from this module
]

???
* The continuity slide — closes the Bridge Module
* The right column is also a self-test for students: if these items feel uncomfortable, revisit Sessions 1–3 before ER017

## Reading list — curated

These are the references that have actually shaped Sessions 1–3, in order of accessibility.

.pull-left[
### `r fa('book-open-reader', fill='#D50006')` Start here
* **`r Citet(bib, "huntington-klein_effect_2025")`** — *The Effect: An Introduction to Research Design and Causality.* The single best gentle introduction. Free online: theeffectbook.net
* **`r Citet(bib, "taddy_modern_2023")`** — *Modern Business Analytics.* The data-science-first econometrics reference; matches our DGP-first frame
* `r Citet(bib, "shmueli_2010")` — the foundational explain-vs-predict article

### `r fa('book', fill='#502479')` For depth on causal inference
* **`r Citet(bib, "cunningham_2021")`** — *Causal Inference: The Mixtape.* DAGs, design-based methods, code in R/Stata. Free online: mixtape.scunning.com
* `r Citet(bib, "angrist_pischke_2009")` — *Mostly Harmless Econometrics.* The credibility-revolution classic
]

.pull-right[
### `r fa('book-bookmark', fill='#7d0a52')` For depth on prediction
* `r Citet(bib, "taddy_modern_2023")` — modern textbook reference
* `r Citet(bib, "tibshirani_1996")` (Lasso); `r Citet(bib, "hastie_tibshirani_friedman_2009")` (ESL)
* `r Citet(bib, "fan_bigdata_2014")` — the big-data regression problems

### `r fa('flask', fill='#D50006')` Frontier
* `r Citet(bib, "chernozhukov_DoubleML_2018")` — Double Machine Learning
* `r Citet(bib, "borusyak_etal_2024")` — modern DiD
* `r Citet(bib, "spiess_optimalEstimation_2025")` — credibility as institutional discipline
* `r Citet(bib, "mullainathan_MLApplied_2017")` — ML meets econometrics
* `r Citet(bib, "athey_imbens_2019")` — the ML/econometrics interface
* `r Citet(bib, "holland_1986")`; `r Citet(bib, "pearl_2009")` — foundations
]
